To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mitochondrial transcription factor A (MTF), a mitochondrial protein released from damaged cells, binds to and activates plasmacytoidal dendritic cells (PDCs), and thereby triggers an immune response.
mitochondrial TFAM, a mitochondrial DNA binding protein, augments CpG DNA-mediated TNFα release by plasmacytold dendritic cells via a receptor complex that involves RAGE and TRL9.
mitochondrial transcription factor A, an endogenous danger signal, promotes TNFα release via RAGE- (and TLR9)-responsive plasmacytold dendritic cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of mitochondria in the innate immune response, and in particular, how the release of mtDNA and mitochondrial proteins can activate the innate immune system.
understanding how the innate immune system recognizes and responds to mitochondrial danger signals.
the role of mitochondrial transcription factor A ( TFAM ) in sterile inflammation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
TFAM is a novel danger signal that, in concert with TLR9, promotes the release of TNFα from RAGE-expressing pDCs via an ECE-1 dependent mechanism.
the TFAM-CGp DNA complex, which represents a mitochondrial danger signal, activates TLR9 signaling in endosomes via RAGE and ECE-1 to promote TNFα release.
TFAM is an endogenous danger signal that promotes TNFα release by RAGE and/or TLR9-responsive cells, including pDCs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
TFAM is a potent endogenous danger signal capable of promoting TNFα release through a TLR9-RAGE-dependent pathway.
the RAGE ligand TFAM promotes TNFα release via TLR9-responsive pDCs, with ECE-1 playing a critical role in TLR9 signaling.
TFAM, released from damaged mitochondria, is a danger signal capable of promoting a proinflammatory immune response by engaging RAGE and TLF9-responsive pDCs.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the RAGE and TLF9 receptors, in concert, amplify sterile inflammatory responses to TFAM released from damaged cells, and that this process is regulated, in part, by endothelin converting enzyme 1 (ECE1) and heparin sulfate.
TFAM, a mitochondrial protein that is released from dying or damaged cells and is bound to mitochondrial DNA, can promote the release of TNFα from splenocytes in a TLR9- and RAGE-dependent manner.
TFAM, a danger signal released from damaged cells, is recognized by TLR9-ex- pressing pDCs, which then release TNFα.
